title: Sikhism: share
hook: share what you earn with others

segments.voice: Yesterday: kirat karni, and the carpenter's bread. Your line was honest work. Which piece of work did you do fully and cleanly? Day two hundred seventy-seven.

A father gives his teenage son twenty rupees, a real sum, and sends him to the market with one instruction: make a good deal. Buy something you can sell for a profit. Learn the family business. The boy sets off. On the road he meets a group of holy men who haven't eaten in days. He spends every rupee on food for them, and comes home empty-handed. His father is furious. The boy is calm. He says he made the truest deal there is. The boy was the young Nanak. Today, on our visit to Sikhism: vand chhakna, sharing.
screen: `TWENTY RUPEES AND ONE INSTRUCTION.` → `HUNGRY MEN ON THE ROAD.` → `THE TRUEST DEAL.`

segments.voice: That story, like yesterday's, comes from the janamsakhis, and Sikhs call it sacha sauda, the true bargain. A gurdwara stands today at the place where tradition says it happened. It's a picture of the third pillar of Sikh life: vand chhakna, to share and consume together. Vand means dividing, sharing out. Chhakna means eating, partaking. Share what you have, then enjoy it, together. Notice how the three pillars fit. Remember the name. Earn honestly. Share what you earn. Yesterday's hymn at Ang 1245 holds the last two in one breath: the one who eats what he earns by his own effort, and gives some of it away, recognizes the path. Honest work without sharing can turn into hoarding. Sharing without honest work isn't really yours to give. Sikhs made this concrete. Sikh tradition asks for dasvandh, setting aside a tenth of one's income for the community and those in need, a practice that grew under the later Gurus. Sharing also means time and skill, not only money. Sikhs call selfless service seva, and you'll see it in any gurdwara: people cleaning shoes, sweeping floors, chopping onions, who may spend the rest of the week as doctors, drivers or shopkeepers. And a kitchen where everyone eats together is tomorrow's story. The deeper idea is that everything comes from the one creator we met three days ago, so nothing is entirely private property. Sharing isn't charity from above. It's handing around what was always meant to go around.
screen: `SACHA SAUDA — THE TRUE BARGAIN.` · `VAND — SHARE. CHHAKNA — PARTAKE.` · `EARN, THEN GIVE SOME AWAY.` · `DASVANDH — A TENTH.` · then, large: `SHARE IT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: think about a meal. Sit, and think of what you'll eat today. Now think of who you could share it with: a coworker at lunch, a neighbor, a friend who's struggling, a stranger outside the shop. Picture handing it over, and picture eating together if you can. Notice any reluctance, and let it soften. The bell holds the time.
Vand chhakna. Share and partake: the third pillar of Sikh life, giving some of what you honestly earn. Today's word.
Your line: share it. Today, share food with one person, and if you can, sit and eat it together. Day two hundred seventy-seven.

howItsDone: Many Sikhs set aside dasvandh, a tenth of their income, for the community and those in need, and give time as seva in the gurdwara, from cleaning to cooking for the shared meal.
